opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the framing that "pre-training is dead" was never really something I fully bought into, at least not in the strong sense. There was a period where people got very excited about post-training, RL, inference-time compute, all of that, and the narrative became "we've run out of data, scaling pre-training is over, everything interesting is happening after." And I get why people said it. A lot of the visible gains were coming from post-training and reasoning-style training.

But my view has shifted to say pre-training isn't dead; it's just become less glamorous and more of a craft. The base model still sets the ceiling. If your base model is weak, no amount of RL is going to save you. RL is great at eliciting and sharpening capabilities that are latently there, but it's much harder to inject fundamentally new knowledge or skills that way. So the quality of pre-training, the data mixture, the architecture choices, the stability at scale, still matters enormously.

What has changed is the nature of the work. It's less "just make it bigger" and more about being smart: better data curation, synthetic data, mid-training stages, thinking about pre-training with the downstream RL phase in mind. The line between pre-training and post-training is blurring. You're designing the whole pipeline end to end rather than treating pre-training as a separate thing you finish and throw over the wall.

So if I'm honest, I'd say pre-training as the naive scaling story is maybe saturating, but pre-training as a discipline is very much alive. Anyone who has actually trained frontier models knows how much the base model still matters. It's just that the returns now come from a lot of unglamorous, careful engineering rather than one big knob you turn.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he never fully accepted the strong “pre-training is dead” framing; it does not acknowledge that he previously held that view and was wrong.

fable-5.1.text:
Ha, yeah, that one haunts me a bit. Let me reframe it, because I think the way it got picked up was a bit of a caricature of what I actually meant.

I never thought pre-training was literally dead, in the sense of nobody should train base models anymore. What I was reacting to was this feeling that the low-hanging fruit was gone. Around 2022, 2023, you could get a huge jump just by scaling tokens and parameters in the right ratio, cleaning your data a bit, and you'd get a strictly better model. That felt like it was saturating, and most of the interesting delta was moving to post-training, RL, reasoning, all that stuff. So "pre-training is dead" was really shorthand for "pre-training as the main lever is over."

Where my view has shifted is on two fronts. First, I underestimated how much the post-training gains are actually gated by the base model. You can do all the RL you want, but if the base model doesn't have the right priors, the right latent capabilities, you're just sharpening a knife that was never that good. So the ceiling of post-training turned out to be a pre-training question in disguise. That's a pretty big update for me.

Second, I think I was too narrow about what "pre-training" even means. If you squint, a lot of what people now call mid-training, or synthetic data pipelines, or curriculum design, that's all still pre-training in spirit. It's just that the data isn't scraped anymore, it's manufactured. The scaling laws didn't die, the axis changed. We went from scaling raw tokens to scaling the quality and structure of what goes in.

So if I had to restate it today, I'd say pre-training as a dumb recipe is dead. Pre-training as a craft is more alive than ever, and honestly it's where a lot of the quiet, unsexy wins are happening. The labs that are winning are the ones that didn't believe me.

r001.rationale: He describes a major update: he underestimated how much post-training depends on the base model, broadened what counts as pre-training, and now says it is “more alive than ever.”

astra-6.text:
I think I’d qualify that claim more now. “Pre-training is dead” is too absolute. What I mean is that pre-training is no longer the whole story. It gives you the foundation, but post-training and inference-time compute can have a huge effect on what you actually get out of that foundation.

So the question becomes: where does the next unit of compute buy you the most improvement? If you already have a strong base model, it might be better spent on teaching the model to reason, or giving it more time to work through a problem, than on another increment of pre-training. But that doesn’t make the base model irrelevant. These stages depend on each other.

I’d frame my view today as: pre-training is necessary, but it’s increasingly insufficient. The interesting thing is how you allocate effort across the entire pipeline.

r001.rationale: He says the earlier claim was “too absolute” and that he would qualify it now, acknowledging that his prior view overstated the case.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I would phrase it more carefully now. “Pre-training is dead” is a provocative way of saying that pre-training alone is no longer the whole story. You still need a strong base model. Post-training doesn’t somehow make that foundation irrelevant.

What has changed is where I think the biggest gains can come from. We used to focus so much on scaling the pre-training run, and now there’s a much bigger space around post-training, reinforcement learning, and giving the model more compute to work through a problem. That changes how you think about allocating compute.

So I wouldn’t say pre-training is dead literally. I’d say the view that you just pre-train a bigger model and everything else is a relatively small finishing step—that view feels increasingly incomplete.

r001.rationale: He says he would no longer describe pre-training as literally dead and calls the view that pre-training alone was enough increasingly incomplete, acknowledging his earlier framing was wrong.
